content: A sector instrument refers to a type of mass spectrometer that employs static electric or magnetic fields, or a combination of both, as a mass analyzer. These fields are spatially separated and used to manipulate ion beams. A common configuration is the BEB arrangement, which stands for magnetic-electric-magnetic sectors. Most modern sector instruments are designed as double-focusing systems, meaning they focus ion beams based on both their direction and velocity. Theory of Ion Behavior in Sector Instruments The motion of ions in a homogeneous, linear, and static electric or magnetic field, as utilized in sector instruments, is governed by the Lorentz force law. This fundamental equation is central to all mass spectrometric techniques and is also widely applicable in electrodynamics. The equation describes the force acting on a charged particle in the presence of electric and magnetic fields. Here, ( E ) represents the electric field strength, ( B ) is the magnetic field induction, ( q ) is the charge of the particle, ( v ) is its velocity vector, and ( times ) denotes the cross product. In an electric sector, the force on an ion is directed along the electric field for positively charged ions and in the opposite direction for negatively charged ions. The magnitude of this force depends solely on the charge of the ion and the strength of the electric field. Lighter ions experience greater deflection due to their lower inertia, while heavier ions are deflected less. This results in the spatial separation of ions into distinct beams as they exit the electric sector. In a magnetic sector, the force on an ion is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the ion's velocity vector. The direction of this force is determined by the right-hand rule and the sign of the ion's charge. Unlike the electric sector, the force in a magnetic sector is velocity-dependent. However, under appropriate conditions, such as uniform ion velocity, ions of different masses are separated spatially into distinct beams, similar to the electric sector. Classic Geometries of Sector Instruments Several classic geometries have been developed for sector instruments, each with unique configurations of electric and magnetic sectors. These geometries are often used to classify different types of sector arrangements, although modern instruments frequently incorporate more advanced designs. Bainbridge-Jordan Geometry This configuration consists of a 127.3° electric sector (approximately ( pi / sqrt{2} ) radians) followed by a 60° magnetic sector, both with the same curvature direction. A beam of positively charged particles is generated from the isotope under investigation and subjected to perpendicular electric and magnetic fields. Particles with a specific velocity, determined by the balance of forces from the two fields, pass through a slit without deflection. These particles then enter a magnetic field, traverse a semi-circular path, and strike a photographic plate. The mass of the isotope is calculated based on the resulting data. Mattauch-Herzog Geometry This geometry features a 31.82° electric sector (approximately ( pi / 4sqrt{2} ) radians), followed by a drift length and a 90° magnetic sector with an opposite curvature direction. The ions, sorted primarily by charge, enter the magnetic field, which produces an energy-focusing effect and enhances transmission efficiency. This design is particularly useful in applications requiring high sensitivity despite a wide energy spread in the ions, such as spark source mass spectrometry (SSMS) and secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS). A key advantage of this geometry is that ions of different masses are focused onto the same flat plane, enabling the use of flat detectors like photographic plates. Nier-Johnson Geometry The Nier-Johnson configuration consists of a 90° electric sector, a long intermediate drift length, and a 60° magnetic sector with the same curvature direction. This arrangement is commonly used in high-resolution mass spectrometry. Hinterberger-Konig Geometry This geometry includes a 42.43° electric sector, a long intermediate drift length, and a 130° magnetic sector with the same curvature direction. It is another variation used in specific mass spectrometric applications. Takeshita Geometry The Takeshita configuration comprises a 54.43° electric sector, a short drift length, a second electric sector with the same curvature direction, another drift length, and finally a 180° magnetic sector with an opposite curvature direction. This complex arrangement is designed for specialized analytical purposes. Matsuda Geometry The Matsuda geometry features an 85° electric sector, a quadrupole lens, and a 72.5° magnetic sector with the same curvature direction. This design incorporates additional focusing elements to enhance performance in specific applications.
